name: JtR - Crack Password-Protected Files (2john)
description: The *2john helpers convert a protected artifact (SSH key, Office doc, PDF, ZIP) into a John-crackable hash. Extract the hash, crack it with a wordlist, then reveal the password with --show. Locate all helpers with 'locate *2john*'.

examples.label: SSH key -> hash (system tool, preferred over ssh2john.py script)
CAUTION: hashcat fails for SSH hashes with 'Token length exception' — use john instead
examples.command:
# hashcat -m 22921 ssh.hash wordlist   ← may fail: 'Token length exception / No hashes loaded'
# john --wordlist=ssh.passwords --rules=sshRules ssh.hash   ← john handles SSH correctly

notes: Check whether an SSH key is even encrypted first: ssh-keygen -yf <keyfile> prompts for a passphrase only if it is. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 15 (Password Attacks).

recommended.note: Cracks hashes with John the Ripper.
Runs a straight dictionary attack (-a 0): each wordlist entry is hashed and compared to the target.

variations.label: SSH Key
variations.command:
ssh2john.py <keyfile> > ssh.hash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh.hash
john ssh.hash --show

variations.label: Office Doc
variations.command:
office2john.py <file> > office.hash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt office.hash
john office.hash --show

variations.label: PDF
variations.command:
pdf2john.py <file> > pdf.hash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt pdf.hash
john pdf.hash --show

variations.label: ZIP Archive
variations.command:
zip2john <file> > zip.hash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt zip.hash
john zip.hash --show

defense.why_it_works: The *2john tools (zip2john, office2john, ssh2john, pdf2john, etc.) extract a crackable hash from a password-protected file for offline attack.
defense.prerequisites: The protected file and the matching *2john extractor + a wordlist.
defense.impact: A hash whose cracking reveals the file's password and contents.
defense.prevention: Strong passphrases on protected files; the attack is offline and undetectable, so passphrase strength is the only defence.
defense.misconfiguration: Authentication protocols store or transmit passwords in formats that are offline-crackable: NTLM hashes (no salt, fast GPU attack), NTLMv2 net hashes (slightly slower but crackable), Kerberos RC4 hashes from Kerberoasting (offline crack without network contact), MD5/SHA1 web app hashes (no key stretching). Weak passwords crack in minutes; even complex ones crack with sufficient GPU power if hashing is fast.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# NTLM hash — no salt, instantaneous lookup with rainbow tables:
# Hash: aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c
# 'password' -> hash computed in microseconds (MD4 algorithm)
# 4x RTX 3090 GPUs: ~300 GH/s NTLM = 8-char complex password cracks in hours

# Web app MD5 password storage:
# $password = md5($_POST['password']);
# Bcrypt would take 1000x longer per attempt for attacker
defense.secure_config:
# Web apps — use bcrypt/Argon2 (adaptive, memory-hard):
import bcrypt
# Hashing:
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12))
# Verification (slow by design):
bcrypt.checkpw(password.encode(), hashed)

# Python — Argon2 (winner of Password Hashing Competition):
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536, parallelism=4)
hash = ph.hash(password)
ph.verify(hash, password)
